question: In H-Net, how does the routing module compute boundary probabilities $p_t$ and discrete boundary indicators $b_t$, and what is the formula and weight $\alpha$ for the auxiliary ratio loss $\mathcal{L}_{\text{ratio}}$?
expected: The routing module projects encoder outputs $\hat{x}_t$ into queries $q_t = W_q\hat{x}_t$ and keys $k_t = W_k\hat{x}_t$, computing scaled cosine dissimilarity between adjacent positions: $p_t = \frac{1}{2}\left(1 - \frac{q_t^\top k_{t-1}}{\|q_t\|\|k_{t-1}\|}\right) \in [0,1]$, with $p_1 = 1.0$ by definition (the sequence begins with a boundary), and sets boundary indicator $b_t = \mathbf{1}_{\{p_t \ge 0.5\}}$ (Dynamic Chunking / H-Net, Sec. 2.2.1, Eq. 4). To guide compression toward target downsampling ratio $N$, H-Net adds the ratio loss $\mathcal{L}_{\text{ratio}} = \frac{N}{N-1}\left((N-1)FG + (1-F)(1-G)\right)$, where $F = \frac{1}{L}\sum_{t=1}^L b_t$ is the fraction of vectors selected and $G = \frac{1}{L}\sum_{t=1}^L p_t$ is the mean boundary probability; it is added to the autoregressive loss as $\mathcal{L} = \mathcal{L}_{\text{AR}} + \alpha\sum_{s=0}^{S-1}\mathcal{L}_{\text{ratio}}^s$ with $\alpha = 0.03$ fixed in all experiments (Sec. 2.2.3, Eq. 10).

question: At the XL (1.3B) scale on FineWeb-Edu, after how many training bytes do H-Net (space), H-Net (1-stage), and H-Net (2-stage) cross over the BPE-tokenized Transformer in bits-per-byte (BPB), and what are their final validation BPB and Robustness Scores?
expected: At the GPT-3 XL scale, byte-level H-Net (space), H-Net (1-stage), and H-Net (2-stage) overtake the BPE-tokenized Transformer after $200\text{B}$, $100\text{B}$, and $30\text{B}$ training bytes, respectively (Dynamic Chunking / H-Net, Sec. 1, Sec. 3.1, Fig. 3). Their final FineWeb-Edu validation BPB scores are $0.726$ for H-Net (space), $0.728$ for H-Net (1-stage), and $0.715$ for H-Net (2-stage), beating the BPE Transformer's $0.730$ (Table 2). On perturbed HellaSwag, their Robustness Scores are $40.5$, $39.5$, and $42.8$, respectively, compared to just $22.2$ for the BPE Transformer (Table 3).

question: How does H-Net make discrete chunking and decompression differentiable during training, and which of the three ablated DC components (smoothing module, cosine routing, or STE) has the largest impact on training stability?
expected: During decompression, H-Net's smoothing module applies a causal exponential moving average $\bar{z}_t = P_t\hat{z}_t + (1-P_t)\bar{z}_{t-1}$ over compressed chunks (Dynamic Chunking / H-Net, Sec. 2.2.2, Eq. 5), and the upsampler weights causally expanded vectors $\tilde{z}_t = \bar{z}_{\sum_{k=1}^t b_k}$ by $\text{STE}(c_t) = c_t + \text{stopgradient}(1-c_t)$, where confidence $c_t = p_t^{b_t}(1-p_t)^{1-b_t}$ rounds to $1.0$ in the forward pass while passing continuous gradients in the backward pass (Sec. 2.2.2, Eq. 6–9). In the Section 3.3 ablation study (Figure 7), the smoothing module is by far the most critical component: removing it (w/o smoothing) causes severe fluctuations in stage compression ratios $L^{s+1}/L^s$ and the largest degradation in validation BPB, whereas cosine routing and STE provide secondary stability and performance gains (Sec. 3.3, Fig. 7).
reply: H-Net makes discrete chunking differentiable by inserting a smoothing module that replaces hard chunk boundaries with an exponential moving average, thereby turning the discrete upsampling operation into a continuous, differentiable computation that allows gradients to flow through boundary decisions [hnet-C-014]. It further introduces a straight‑through estimator (STE) in the upsampler that rounds confidence scores to 1.0 during the forward pass while preserving continuous gradients during back‑propagation, and it weights the decompression step by confidence scores so that confident boundary predictions receive direct gradient feedback [hnet-C-015]. Among the three ablated dynamic‑chunking components, the smoothing module has the largest impact on training stability; removing it causes severe fluctuations in compression ratios and prevents the model from learning consistent chunk‑boundary patterns, leading to substantial performance degradation [hnet-C-042].
citations: H-Net v2, §2.2.2 Dechunking | H-Net v2, §3.3 Ablation Studies

question: How does enabling Inner Monologue affect Moshi's spoken question answering accuracy across Web Questions, LlaMA-Questions, and Audio TriviaQA, and how can the same architecture be switched into streaming ASR or streaming TTS without changing the loss or architecture?
expected: Enabling Inner Monologue nearly triples Moshi's 0-shot spoken QA accuracy: Web Questions jumps from $9.2\%$ to $26.6\%$, LlaMA-Questions from $21.0\%$ to $62.3\%$, and Audio TriviaQA from $7.3\%$ to $22.8\%$, while only increasing per-step token predictions from 16 to 17 (Moshi, Sec. 5.5, Table 8). By adjusting a single delay hyperparameter between the text stream ($W_t$) and audio tokens ($A_{t,q}$), Moshi becomes a streaming ASR system when text tokens are delayed by $2\text{ seconds}$ behind teacher-forced input audio tokens ($5.7\%$ WER on LibriSpeech test-clean with $80\text{ ms}$ word alignment precision), or a streaming TTS system when audio tokens are delayed by $2\text{ seconds}$ behind teacher-forced text tokens ($4.7\%$ WER on LibriSpeech test-clean, beating Vall-E's $5.9\%$) (Sec. 3.4.4, Sec. 5.7, Appendix C).
reply: Enabling Inner Monologue dramatically improves Moshi’s spoken question‑answering accuracy, almost tripling performance on all three benchmarks compared to a model trained without the method; for example, Moshi with Inner Monologue scores 26.6 % on Web Questions, 62.3 % on LlaMA‑Questions, and 22.8 % on Audio TriviaQA, whereas the same architecture without Inner Monologue achieves only 9.2 %, 21.0 %, and 7.3 % respectively (Table 8) [moshi-C-052]. The same multi‑stream architecture can be repurposed for streaming ASR or streaming TTS simply by adjusting the delay between text and audio tokens—no change to the loss function or the underlying model is required—because Inner Monologue’s prefix‑generation framework is compatible with any streaming inference setup [moshi-C-077].

question: Why does H-Net use Mamba-2 layers for its outer encoder and decoder networks ($\mathcal{E}^s, \mathcal{D}^s$) on text and code, yet find a hybrid M3T1 encoder superior on the HG38 DNA benchmark?
expected: In H-Net, outer encoders and decoders operate on long, uncompressed sequences. Section 3.3 ablations (M4-M4 vs. T2-T2 on both raw bytes and BPE tokens, Figures 8–10) show that pure Transformer encoders/decoders (T2-T2) perform worst and compress poorly even at higher FLOPs because Transformers store full KV caches, whereas Mamba-2 state-space models have an inherent inductive bias for compressing sequential context into fixed-size states (Dynamic Chunking / H-Net, Sec. 2.1.2, Sec. 3.3). However, on the human genome dataset (HG38), an M3T1 encoder (3 Mamba-2 + 1 Transformer layer) outperforms a pure M4 encoder ($2.705$ vs. $2.722$ perplexity with a T15 main network, and $2.697$ vs. $2.706$ with an M15 main network), and adding flanking Transformer layers (T1M13T1) in the main network eliminates loss spikes—a modality-specific effect on base-pair sequences (Sec. 3.2, Table 5, Appendix E.3, Table 7, Fig. 14).

question: How does Post-Training Quantization (PTQ) from BF16 down to W8A8, W4A8, and W2A8 (block size 32) affect MMLU for Helium versus instructed Moshi, and how does Moshi detect audio artifacts like gibberish, repetitive text, and background noise using token entropy?

Instructed multi-stream Moshi is more sensitive linguistically: MMLU drops from $49.7$ (BF16A8) to $47.6$ (W8A8, deployed in the online demo), $42.2$ (W4A8), and $24.9$ (W2A8) (Table 11b). Because MOSNet fails to capture low-bitwidth audio artifacts, Moshi computes Shannon entropy $H_i^0$ (text) and $H_i^k$ (audio) over sliding windows of $C=64$ tokens across non-overlapping $\omega=64$-token intervals: repetitive text has flat, non-zero text entropy (linear regression slope $<\eta_{\text{flat}}=10^{-3}$); background noise has silent text ($H^0=0$) but median audio entropy $>\eta_{\text{audio\_silence}}=2$; gibberish has text entropy $H^0 > \eta_{\text{gibberish}}=3.5$; and noisy audio has standard deviation of entropy across audio codebooks $>\eta_{\text{noise}}=0.6$ (Sec. 5.8, Table 12, Appendix D).

question: Compare how "Encoder" and "Decoder" modules are architected—including layer counts, layer types, and normalization placement—across the original Transformer, Moshi's Mimi codec, and a 1-stage Large H-Net.
expected: 1) Original Transformer (Attention Is All You Need, Sec. 3.1): Both Encoder and Decoder consist of $N=6$ identical Transformer layers ($d_{\text{model}}=512$, $h=8$, $d_{ff}=2048$) using post-normalization $\text{LayerNorm}(x + \text{Sublayer}(x))$. 2) Moshi's Mimi Codec (Moshi, Sec. 3.3.1): The encoder and decoder are causal SeaNet convolutional networks (4 strided/transposed-strided blocks with ELU and Weight Normalization) augmented with an 8-layer, 8-head causal Transformer bottleneck ($d=512$, MLP $2048$, GELU, RoPE, LayerScale init $0.01$) right before and after RVQ. 3) 1-Stage Large H-Net (Dynamic Chunking / H-Net, Sec. 2.1.2, Sec. 2.3, Table 1): The outer encoder $\mathcal{E}^0$ and decoder $\mathcal{D}^0$ each use 4 Mamba-2 layers without MLPs ($D^0=1024$) around a 22-layer Transformer main network ($D^1=1536$), using pre-normalization plus a final RMSNorm at the end of $\mathcal{E}^s$, $\mathcal{D}^s$, and $\mathcal{M}$ ("Norm Balance") and a zero-initialized Linear projection on the encoder-to-decoder residual stream.

question: In Moshi's safety evaluation, why does AudioSeal signal-based watermarking fail when tested against Mimi, why does token-level generative watermarking also fail, and how does Moshi eliminate verbatim training-data regurgitation?
expected: When AudioSeal-watermarked audio is compressed and decompressed through Mimi (or RVQGAN), the 10-second watermark detection score collapses from $0.9999$ to $0.0805$ ($0.2404$ on 1-minute audio), which is indistinguishable from unwatermarked audio ($0.0855$ / $0.2474$) because low-bitrate perceptual codecs discard non-reconstructive signal perturbations (Moshi, Sec. 6.4, Table 15). Generative token-sampling watermarks also fail because Mimi is not idempotent: re-encoding a generated waveform changes token indices (even at $\Delta T = 0$, only $76.6\%$ of semantic $k=1$ tokens and $26.4\%–55.0\%$ of acoustic $k=2..8$ tokens match, dropping to $48.3\%$ for $k=1$ under a $40\text{ ms}$ shift) (Sec. 6.4, Table 16). To prevent regurgitation of frequent training segments (which reaches $98.4\%–100\%$ on 3s-prompted raw single-stream models), Moshi deduplicates the training audio using mel-spectrogram constellation-map hashes ($2^{26}$ hash space with Hough 1D temporal voting, Appendix B), reducing the regurgitation rate to $0.00\%$ across $10^5$ generations (Sec. 6.2, Table 13, Appendix B).
